verification_note: Each fact below was checked against the cited fact-check page on 2026-10-16. Snopes pages returned HTTP 402 to our fetcher, so Snopes findings are taken as relayed by the cited outlets and carry lower confidence. Conflicts between sources are recorded, not resolved.

sources.name: 2012 'days of darkness' chain email (Mayan-calendar apocalypse rumor)

claims.text: NASA confirmed the Earth will go completely dark for three days in December 2012.
claims.evidence: Snopes (science/astronomy/blackout) collected a chain email claiming NASA confirmed three days of darkness on December 5th 2012; Inverse (2017-11-02) reports Snopes traced the darkness hoax back to the 2012 Mayan-calendar apocalypse rumor.

claims.text: NASA confirms the Earth will have six days of almost complete darkness, December 16 to 22, 2014, caused by a solar storm.
claims.evidence: ThatsNonsense (2014-10-27) and EarthSky (2014-12-01): Huzlers story, darkness Tuesday 16th to Monday 22nd December, solar storm filling the sky with dust and debris.

claims.text: NASA confirms the Earth will have six days of almost complete darkness in June 2015, caused by a solar storm.
claims.evidence: ThatsNonsense (2014-10-27, updated 2016-10-24): copycat sites anonymousmags.com and theracketreport.com reposted near-identical versions with the date changed to June 2015. Posting dates not given.

claims.text: NASA confirms the Earth will have 15 days of complete darkness from November 15 to 29, 2015.
claims.evidence: PolitiFact (2017-06-14): YourNewsWire.com, Oct. 22, 2015. St Thomas Source (2015-10-27), quoting Snopes: Newswatch33, 15 days of total darkness between November 15 and November 29.

claims.text: NASA confirms the Earth will have 15 days of total darkness from November 15 to 29, 2016.
claims.evidence: PolitiFact (2017-06-14): GlobalRevolutionNetwork.com, Oct. 24, 2016 (per Internet Archive). ThatsNonsense (2016-10-24) quotes naturalmedicineworld.com: total darkness for 15 days in November 2016.

claims.text: NASA's confirmed 15 days of darkness in November 2016 is proof that the Bible is accurate and a sign of the end times.
claims.evidence: ThatsNonsense (2016-10-24): some variants claim the darkness is proof the Holy Bible is accurate and a sign of the end of times. Publisher not named.

claims.text: NASA confirms the Earth will have 15 days of darkness in November 2017; NASA's administrator sent a 1,000-page document explaining it to the White House.
claims.evidence: FactCheck.org (2017-08-11): reflectionofmind.org and globalrevolutionnetwork.com, Jan. 12 [2017]; twofeed.org, May 29, 2017; stories claim Charles Bolden wrote a 1000-page document for the White House. PolitiFact (2017-06-14): NewsForMeToday.com, June 2, 2017, citing ReflectionofMind.org (Jan. 12, 2017).

sightings.date_note: Chain email; the email itself says NASA confirmed it on December 5th 2012.

sightings.snippet: Satire site story: NASA says six days of near-total darkness, December 16-22, from a solar storm.

mutations.before_text: three days of darkness in December 2012
mutations.note: CONTESTED link. Snopes (as relayed by Inverse) traces the hoax back to the 2012 rumor; ThatsNonsense and EarthSky name Huzlers as the origin without mentioning 2012.
ThatsNonsense: near-identical copies with the date changed. Posting date unknown, so direction is not certain from dates alone.
ThatsNonsense (2016, 2017) treats the six-day and 15-day stories as one long-running hoax with changed durations and dates.

mutations.after_text: 15 days of darkness in November 2016, proof the Bible is accurate and a sign of the end times
mutations.note: Added religious end-times framing. No enum type fits exactly; 'exaggeration' is the closest. Flagged for owner review in DECISIONS.md.

mutations.after_text: 15 days of darkness in November 2017; NASA's administrator sent a 1,000-page document to the White House
mutations.note: Fact-checks document the 1,000-page White House document only in 2017 versions; it may have appeared earlier.

origins.note: ThatsNonsense (2014, 2016, 2017) and EarthSky name Huzlers.com as where the hoax started.

origins.target: 2012 'days of darkness' chain email (Mayan-calendar apocalypse rumor)
origins.note: Snopes (relayed by Inverse, 2017-11-02) traces the rumor to 2012 and the Mayan-calendar apocalypse. Snopes page not fetched directly.

fact_checks.summary: Rated Pants on Fire: no evidence NASA made any such announcement; the story is completely made up.
NASA made no such announcement; no evidence of the 1,000-page document.
The latest version of a long-running hoax; it has never been true.
Hoax: NASA confirmed no such thing.
News coverage relaying Snopes: Newswatch33 is not a legitimate news outlet and the story recycles an older debunked rumor.
Total nonsense: NASA published no such report.
No such darkness was predicted; NASA Earth Observatory disavowed the claim.
